tool.name: TileEdgeConsistencyChecker
tool.summary: Checks the seams of tiled data. Give a tile or sheet index (polygons) and one or more feature layers: the tool finds the edges the tiles share and reports, as one error point each, line ends that stop at an edge with no counterpart on the neighbouring tile (DANGLING_END), line ends on the two sides that do not meet (END_OFFSET, with the measured distance), lines that run past the edge instead of stopping at it (OVERSHOOT), paired features whose chosen attributes differ (ATTRIBUTE_MISMATCH), polygon halves with no partner, halves that do not meet at the edge or pieces cut into slivers (POLYGON_UNMATCHED, POLYGON_GAP, POLYGON_SLIVER), points stored twice on both sides (POINT_DUPLICATE), features that cross an edge without being cut (EDGE_CROSSING, optional) and overlapping tiles (TILE_OVERLAP). A second table has one row per shared edge with its counts and a status, so the seams can be mapped. Read-only. Designed for a Basic licence: it calls no Advanced or extension tool.

param.name: in_tiles
param.dialogReference: Polygon layer with the tiles, map sheets or work units.

param.name: tile_id_field
param.dialogReference: Optional field that names the tiles in the outputs. Spaces around a value are removed; an empty or blank value gives 'OID n' ('OID n (no tile ID)' when another tile's ID is the text 'OID n'). A warning is given when two tiles have the same ID.

param.name: in_features
param.dialogReference: Line, polygon or point layers to check along the tile edges.

param.name: compare_fields
param.dialogReference: Optional field names (or aliases) compared across an edge for paired features. A layer without the field is not compared on it. Combined line layers are compared on a listed field even when each stores it under another name or alias.

param.name: checks
param.dialogReference: Checks to run: DANGLING_END, END_OFFSET (gives END_OFFSET and OVERSHOOT), ATTRIBUTE_MISMATCH, POLYGON_PIECE (gives POLYGON_UNMATCHED, POLYGON_GAP and POLYGON_SLIVER), POINT_DUPLICATE, EDGE_CROSSING (off by default).

param.name: tolerance_m
param.dialogReference: Ends (and points) closer than this many metres count as meeting (never less than twice the XY resolution of the inputs; a warning says so when the value is raised, and when the Search Distance is raised with it).

param.name: search_m
param.dialogReference: Farthest distance, in metres, at which a counterpart on the other side is looked for. Must be at least the Match Tolerance.

param.name: edge_m
param.dialogReference: A line end or polygon boundary within this many metres of a shared edge is at the edge (never less than the snap distance). Two polygon halves that are both at the edge but farther apart than the Match Tolerance are POLYGON_GAP.

param.name: adjacency_m
param.dialogReference: Tile boundaries closer than this many metres are the same edge. It is also the snap distance: a line end or point this close to a tile boundary is on it (never less than twice the XY resolution of the inputs).

param.name: sliver_area_m2
param.dialogReference: Polygon pieces at an edge smaller than this many square metres are slivers. 0 = off.

param.name: skip_connected
param.dialogReference: Checked (default): a line end that touches another line of the layer within the Match Tolerance is a junction, not a dangling end, and is not paired with an end farther away than the Match Tolerance. Two junction ends on the two sides of an edge that do not meet (3 m apart, say) are therefore not reported; the run counts such pairs in a warning. This applies to every line check (DANGLING_END, END_OFFSET and ATTRIBUTE_MISMATCH, also when ATTRIBUTE_MISMATCH is the only one), so fewer checks never pair other ends. Unchecked: every edge end without a partner is reported.

param.name: combine_layers
param.dialogReference: Checked: all line layers are one dataset, so a line end of one layer is paired with a line end of another (for data delivered as one layer per tile). Unchecked (default): every layer is checked on its own. Merging the layers first has the same effect.

param.name: out_errors
param.dialogReference: Output point feature class: RULE, LAYER, TILE_A, TILE_B, OFFSET_M, FIELDS, OID_A, OID_B, DETAIL.

param.name: out_summary
param.dialogReference: Output table with one row per shared edge: TILE_A, TILE_B, EDGE_LEN_M, N_ENDS, N_CROSSING, N_MATCHED, N_OFFSET, N_DANGLING, N_ATTR, N_OTHER, STATUS.

param.name: out_edges
param.dialogReference: Optional line feature class with the shared edges and the fields of the edge table.

param.name: out_report
param.dialogReference: Optional Excel (.xlsx) or CSV report with Summary and Detail sheets.

tool.usage:
Quick start. Give the tile index (polygons) and one line layer that holds the lines of all tiles (merge per-tile classes first, or tick Treat Line Layers as One Dataset); run with the defaults; symbolise Output Error Points by RULE and Output Edge Lines by STATUS; read the run messages; untick Skip Line Ends That Touch Another Line to see junction ends.

Prepare the data. The tool pairs the ends of lines that were cut at a tile edge, so the lines of all tiles must be in one layer. If the data comes as one feature class per tile, merge the classes first (Merge) or tick Treat Line Layers as One Dataset; if you give one layer per tile without that option, every layer is checked on its own and every road that crosses a seam is reported as a dangling end on both sides. A line layer listed twice with that option is checked once (the repeat is left out). The run says so in a warning when unpaired ends of one layer coincide with unpaired ends of another layer across a tile edge, and when many unpaired ends sit exactly on tile boundaries.

Tile index. Any polygon layer: a regular grid or an irregular sheet index. Two tiles share an edge where parts of their boundaries run along each other (within the Tile Adjacency Tolerance) for a length above that tolerance, so T-junctions of an irregular index work and tiles that only touch at a corner have no edge. Tiles are found from their boundaries alone. Tiles that overlap are reported as TILE_OVERLAP and the run goes on; the stretches where their boundaries run along each other with the tiles on opposite sides are still checked as edges. The Tile ID Field is used to name tiles in the outputs (the ObjectID when empty). Where two boundaries run close together but do not form a shared edge (a gap between sheets, or a curved boundary drawn with different vertices on the two tiles that differ by more than the adjacency tolerance) nothing is checked along that stretch; the tool counts such tile pairs and warns, naming the largest.

Line ends. The end points of every line part (closed parts have none) are assigned to the tile that contains them. Coordinates are stored on a grid (the XY resolution, 0.0001 m in many geodatabases), so the two ends of a road cut at a tile edge lie a few micrometres on either side of a boundary that is not on the grid. An end within the snap distance of a tile boundary is therefore on it, and is assigned to the tile the line comes from (the first point back along the line that is farther from every boundary than the snap distance). The snap distance is the Tile Adjacency Tolerance, and the adjacency, the Match Tolerance and the Edge Distance are never taken smaller than twice the XY resolution of the inputs (read from their coordinate systems) or, for the Edge Distance, the snap distance. A line that stays within the snap distance of a boundary along its whole length is not assigned. An end within Edge Distance of a shared edge of its tile must have a counterpart: ends of the same layer in different touching tiles are paired one to one, nearest first, when they are within the Search Distance. A pair within the Match Tolerance is consistent; a pair farther apart is END_OFFSET with its distance (OFFSET_M); an edge end with no partner is DANGLING_END. When its nearest end on the other side, within the Search Distance, was already paired with another end (pairs are made nearest first; two ends competing for one), the DANGLING_END names that end in OID_B with its distance in OFFSET_M and says which end it is paired with. A line end that is a real dead end close to a tile edge is reported too; raise or lower Edge Distance to suit the data. A line end that touches another line of the layer (a vertex or a segment within the Match Tolerance, on the same tile as the end; the cut piece on the other side of the seam does not count) is a junction: it is not a dangling end, and it is not paired as an offset against an end farther away than the Match Tolerance, so two junction ends on the two sides of an edge that are 3 m apart are not reported (the run warns how many such pairs it left out; pairs whose two nodes are already joined across the edge by a correctly cut line are not counted, but a connection through several lines is not followed, so the count is a hint to look, and with the filter off such connected nodes do show as END_OFFSET). A free edge end whose nearest end on the other side is such a junction end is DANGLING_END with that end in OID_B and their distance in OFFSET_M (DETAIL: it touches another line there (a junction), so the two were not paired), and that place is not counted in the warning. Untick Skip Line Ends That Touch Another Line to report every unpaired edge end as before. The filter applies to every line check, ATTRIBUTE_MISMATCH included, so a run with fewer checks pairs the same ends as the default run. A missing road whose end would sit exactly on a junction on the seam is therefore not found, and a free dead end can still pair with another dead end across the seam within the Search Distance (END_OFFSET), so keep the Search Distance below the spacing of the lines. A line that comes from the neighbouring tile, passes the edge and ends inside this tile no further beyond the edge than the Edge Distance, measured square to the edge (and more than the snap distance), is an overshoot: its end is also tried as an end of the tile the line comes from. When it pairs with an end on the edge and the two are farther apart than the Match Tolerance the finding is OVERSHOOT (OFFSET_M is how far the end passes the edge, square to the edge whatever the angle of the line; the END_OFFSET check gives both END_OFFSET and OVERSHOOT), not two dangling ends. A deeper overshoot is an uncut line: use EDGE_CROSSING. A line that passes the corner shared by three or four tiles and stops past it in a tile that touches the tile it comes from only at that corner is an overshoot from that diagonal tile (DETAIL: it passes the corner it shares with that tile; OFFSET_M is the distance from the end to the nearest edge of its tile at the corner). Counterparts are looked for in the tiles that touch the end, so a line that is cut exactly at the corner shared by four tiles is paired with the piece in the diagonal tile.

Attributes. List field names or aliases in Fields to Compare; each layer that has the field is compared on it for every pair of line ends, point duplicates and polygon halves. With Treat Line Layers as One Dataset, line ends of two layers are compared on a listed field when both layers have it, also when they store it under different names (CLASS in one layer, Class or a field with the alias CLASS in the other); FIELDS then shows both names (CLASS/Class), and a warning names the line layers without the field. Text is put in canonical Unicode form, invisible marks (bidirectional marks, zero-width space) are dropped, it is trimmed and compared ignoring case; Arabic presentation forms (the lam-alef ligature and the like) equal the letters they stand for; other variants (Arabic and Persian yeh or kaf, alef forms, diacritics, Arabic-Indic digits against Latin digits) are different values; empty text equals null; a date without a time (Date Only field) equals the same day at exactly midnight. Integers must be the same integer, whole-number floats the same number, other floats equal within a relative 1e-9. The mismatching fields are in FIELDS and the values in DETAIL; when two values print the same but are stored as different types (integer 1 and text '1' in combined layers), DETAIL names the types: CLASS: 1 (integer) / '1' (text). Values longer than 40 characters are shortened with '...'; when two long values would then look the same, both are shown from just before the first character where they differ (...lane number 0001 north / ...lane number 0001 south).

Polygons. A polygon piece is a polygon whose boundary runs along a shared edge (within Edge Distance). Pieces on the two sides that overlap along the edge are halves of one cut feature and are compared. Where their facing boundaries are farther apart than the Match Tolerance (a gap between the halves, or one half passing the edge into the other tile) the pair is POLYGON_GAP; OFFSET_M is the largest distance measured across the edge (steps and rectangular notches in the boundaries included) and DETAIL says gap or overlap. A multipart polygon with one part on each side, the parts meeting at the edge, counts as two matched halves. Only the parts of a boundary within the Edge Distance count (a boundary that drifts away from the edge counts up to where it leaves that band, whatever its vertices); where a half is farther away, the other half is POLYGON_UNMATCHED. A piece belongs to the tile on whose side it mostly lies, so a thin strip along the seam is never paired with a polygon of its own tile, and slivers thinner than a millimetre are still found. A piece with a stretch of edge where no polygon of the layer continues is POLYGON_UNMATCHED; a piece smaller than the Sliver Area is POLYGON_SLIVER (0 = off). A polygon that ends at the edge of the data by design is reported as POLYGON_UNMATCHED too.

Points. Two points of one layer in different touching tiles within the Match Tolerance are POINT_DUPLICATE. A point within the snap distance of a tile boundary is on it and belongs to every tile whose boundary it is on; it is paired with points of the neighbouring tile and with other points on the same boundary. Every point on a tile boundary, paired or not, is counted in an information message. Points are paired one to one, nearest first; a copy left over (a point stored in three tiles at a corner) is reported with its nearest copy, so every copy is named in a row.

Crossings. N_CROSSING of the edge table always counts the lines and polygons that pass from one side of an edge to the other inside the edge (a feature through the corner of four tiles counts on each edge that meets the corner); add EDGE_CROSSING to Checks to get an error point for each.

Error points. TILE_A and TILE_B are the two tiles of the edge. For END_OFFSET, POINT_DUPLICATE, ATTRIBUTE_MISMATCH, EDGE_CROSSING and TILE_OVERLAP, TILE_A is the tile that comes first in the tile layer. For POLYGON_GAP, TILE_A is the tile that comes first and OID_A its half. For OVERSHOOT, TILE_A is the tile the overshooting line comes from (OID_A) and TILE_B the tile it runs into (OID_B is the partner). For DANGLING_END, POLYGON_UNMATCHED and POLYGON_SLIVER, TILE_A is the tile the feature (OID_A) is in and TILE_B the tile across the edge. OID_A and OID_B are feature ObjectIDs (OID_B is empty when there is no partner; for DANGLING_END it is the nearest junction end on the other side when there is one, or the nearest end on the other side that was paired with another end); for TILE_OVERLAP they are the ObjectIDs of the two tiles.

Edge table. One row per shared edge (and per pair of overlapping tiles): TILE_A, TILE_B (TILE_A comes first in the tile layer), EDGE_LEN_M, N_ENDS (line ends within Edge Distance of the edge, counted on the nearest edge of their tile), N_CROSSING, N_MATCHED (end pairs within the tolerance and polygon halves), N_OFFSET (END_OFFSET and OVERSHOOT rows), N_DANGLING, N_ATTR, N_OTHER (unmatched, gap or sliver polygons, duplicate points) and STATUS: OK, ISSUES, NO_DATA (nothing reaches the edge) or TILES_OVERLAP. A pair of ends that meets at a corner but not on an edge is counted on the nearest edge. The optional Output Edge Lines has the same fields on the edge geometry, for a map coloured by STATUS.

Size and the Search Distance. The work grows with the number of line ends within the Edge Distance plus the Search Distance of a seam. A Search Distance or Edge Distance near the tile size makes almost every end a candidate: 1,903 road pieces on 3 x 3 tiles of 1 km took 0.2 to 0.7 s with 100 or 250 m, 1.6 s with 400 m, and about 30 to 47 s with 1,000 m before the bound was added. The tool therefore stops when the Search Distance or the Edge Distance is more than a quarter of the typical (median) tile size, and warns above a tenth. Timings are of the checking code alone on the development machine (no cursors, single run, order of magnitude): 176,507 pieces on 10 x 10 tiles of 2 km took about 13 s without and 18 s with the junction filter, at about 500 MB of memory.

Units. All distances are in metres. The tile index must be in a projected coordinate system; geographic (degree) tile indexes and tile indexes with an unknown coordinate system are refused, because a tolerance in metres cannot be applied to degrees. Feature layers in another coordinate system are projected into the tile index system as they are read (a datum difference gives a warning); a layer with an unknown system is refused. Web Mercator distorts distances and gives a warning. Z and M values are ignored and true curves are densified.

Selections and definition queries on the input layers are honoured. The inputs are never edited: an output or report equal to an input is refused. If an arcpy error stops the run while the outputs are written, the outputs this run created are deleted.

Built-in alternatives: Generate Edgematch Links and Edgematch Features (Editing toolbox; the ArcGIS Pro 3.3 tool pages show Basic: No, Standard: No, Advanced: Yes). Generate Edgematch Links takes line features only (Source Features, Adjacent Features, a Search Distance above zero) and writes link lines between matching but disconnected lines, with a confidence value (EM_CONF); its optional Match Fields (pairs of source and adjacent fields) help pick the right match among candidates. Edgematch Features then reshapes lines using those links and edits its input. Those pages do not mention a tile index, polygons, points or counts per edge. This tool edits nothing and runs on Basic. Other Esri products (Production Mapping, Data Reviewer) may offer related checks; they were not compared here.
